tagline.text: A Sunday-morning food market in the heart of Makati's business district

children.text: Legazpi Sunday Market is held in Legazpi Village, Makati, every Sunday from morning until early afternoon. Cooked dishes from around the world, organic produce, desserts and handicrafts gather here, making it a popular spot for a relaxed Sunday brunch in Manila.

Legazpi Sunday Market is a weekend market held every Sunday in Legazpi Village, in Makati's central business district. On weekdays this neighborhood of high-rises and apartment towers is packed with office workers, but on Sunday mornings the parking lot and the area around the park fill with food stalls and residents carrying shopping bags. Together with the Saturday market in neighboring Salcedo Village, it is counted among Makati's best-known weekend markets.

The market's roots go back to 2005 (a June 2026 visit report also calls it the market's 21st year, which fits). According to English Wikipedia, Mara Pardo de Tavera, known as a pioneer of organic markets, started it at Legazpi Active Park as the successor to Mara's Organic Market, which had run at Greenbelt park from 1994 to 2004. That is why many visitors still come for organic vegetables and fruit, natural household products and vegetarian food.

In March 2019 the parking lot next to the park was closed for construction of a multi-level parking building, and the market is reported to have moved temporarily to the Corinthian Plaza parking lot next to the Asian Institute of Management (AIM). Recent travel articles place the market in the Legazpi car park between Corinthian Plaza and Washington SyCip Park. The location may change with construction or events, so please check the market's Facebook or Instagram announcements before you go.

After the pandemic the market came back to life, and as more food stalls opened, tables for eating on the spot were set up as well. With dishes from many countries, such as Moroccan, Turkish, Japanese and Filipino, plus organic ingredients, ice cream and desserts, and general goods like bags, it is not a major sightseeing attraction, but it is a pleasant place to enjoy a casual slice of local Sunday life. Legazpi Village itself is a mixed residential and business district in Makati with plenty of greenery, cafes and apartments. On Sunday mornings there are more residents than tourists, and you will notice families walking their dogs and neighbors with shopping bags. It suits anyone who wants to step away from a mall-and-landmark itinerary and glimpse everyday local life in Manila. If you expect a big sightseeing attraction you may be disappointed, so think of it as a morning meal and a slow stroll.

blocks.title: Cooked dishes from around the world

children.text: What sets this market apart is that you can try cuisines from many countries in one place, not just Filipino food. A March 2024 visit report mentions stalls such as Turkish kofte, Moroccan cooking and saffron plates. The lineup of stalls may change a little from week to week.
The same report lists a newer stall called Adobados, whose tuna adobado (
) is a large chunk of tuna cooked in a coconut-based sauce and served with coconut rice, cucumber and salted egg. The price is as of 2024, so please confirm it on site.

A stall called GINTO Creamery was reported to sell ice cream in Asian-inspired flavors such as Vietnamese coffee, ube halaya, White Rabbit and kaya toast. It makes a fitting dessert after a meal on a Sunday when temperatures rise by midday.

blocks.title: Organic produce and a vegetarian section

children.text: True to its origins as an organic market, vendors sell fresh produce from Luzon and Mindanao and natural personal-care products, and Wikipedia says there is a strictly vegetarian section too. It is also fun to browse tropical fruit and vegetables that are hard to find in Korea.

There are tables in the market, so you can eat what you buy right away. Seating is limited and may be full later in the morning, so go early if you want to sit down. If you are in a group, buying from different stalls and sharing lets you taste the widest variety.
Besides food, some stalls sell bags, plants, handicrafts and household goods. It is a good place to pick up small, easy-to-carry souvenirs.
The market is known to hold occasional morning programs in the form of cultural events, announced on social media. The schedule is not fixed, so check Facebook or Instagram before you visit.

items.title: Sunday morning route
items.subtitle: From browsing the market to a walk in the park

children.text: Arrive around opening time. Sources give slightly different start times,
or
, so there is no need to rush. It is quiet early on, which makes browsing easy.
Walk one full lap to see which stalls are there first. Checking where the lines are long and which dishes are popular before you choose reduces the chance of a miss.
Share two or three dishes as a combined breakfast and brunch. If a table frees up, sit down to eat; with companions, one person can hold a spot while the others bring back food.
Browse organic vegetables, jams and handicrafts and pick out souvenirs. The market winds down around
, but popular dishes sometimes sell out early.
Finish with a stroll through Washington SyCip Park or toward Legazpi Active Park beside the market. On hot days, head to an air-conditioned cafe in a nearby mall.
One to two hours is enough for most travelers. Bring plenty of small bills in cash. On rainy days an umbrella and waterproof shoes are handy, since uncovered areas can get wet.
Have breakfast at Legazpi Sunday Market.
Walk or take a short taxi ride to Greenbelt and look around the park and shopping area.
Have lunch and shop at a restaurant in Greenbelt or Ayala Center.
Relax at a cafe in central Makati or head back to your hotel.
On Sundays some shops and street traffic patterns differ from weekdays, so allow some extra time for getting around.

From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Legazpi Village in Makati, most people take a taxi or Grab. Sunday mornings are usually lighter on traffic than weekdays, but travel time varies a lot with conditions, so check the estimated time in the app.
If you are staying in Makati, enter "Corinthian Plaza, Legazpi Village" as your destination.
The market is in the parking lot area between Corinthian Plaza and Washington SyCip Park, so you can walk there from hotels in Legazpi Village and Salcedo Village.
It is within walking distance of Greenbelt, but on hot days a short taxi or Grab ride is more comfortable.

If you come by taxi, Sunday-morning roads in Makati are relatively quiet, but drop-off spots in the lanes around the market may be restricted. Getting off in front of nearby Corinthian Plaza and walking in is easier.
Central Makati has the MRT-3 Ayala station and several bus routes, but exact routes and walking distances may vary with Sunday service, so please confirm locally.
The market runs on Sundays only. Early in the morning it is cool and quiet; as noon approaches more people arrive and popular dishes start to run out.
The Philippines gets sudden showers in the rainy season, so bring an umbrella, and in the dry season go early to avoid the midday heat.

The market itself is the place for a Sunday breakfast, so you do not need to pick a separate restaurant. The lineup can change from week to week, so first-timers are advised to walk a lap before choosing. Some stalls accept electronic payment besides cash, but it differs by stall, so have cash ready.

If you stay in Legazpi Village, Salcedo Village or the Ayala Avenue area, the market is easy to reach on foot. After the market closes in the afternoon, nearby Greenbelt or Ayala Center are good places to continue with a meal and shopping.

For travelers from Korea, we recommend trying unfamiliar food in small portions, sharing several dishes. Prices are generally similar to or higher than a food court, making it easy to enjoy casually, but they vary widely from stall to stall, so check the price list first. If you are vegetarian, look for the market's vegetarian section or vegetable-focused stalls. Ice cream and desserts melt quickly in hot weather, so eat them right away.
The market runs on Sundays only, usually from
or
until
. Check the latest announcements.
Seating is limited, so arrive early if you want to sit and eat.
Popular stalls sometimes sell out before closing, so go early if there is a dish you want.
Carry cash in small bills, and bring a reusable bag or tote to make buying organic produce easier.
The market may close on public holidays or during typhoons, so check its Facebook or Instagram.
The market's location has changed because of construction before, so search "Legazpi Sunday Market" in a map app to confirm its current location.
The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.

Korean travelers who have been there often leave their Makati hotel early on foot, have breakfast at the market and then walk on toward Greenbelt. On days when you are carrying a lot, drop your things at your hotel right after browsing the market before moving on.
It opens on Sundays only, and its location and hours may change, so check the latest announcements before you leave.
Watch out for pickpockets when it is crowded, and carry your bag in front of you.
The stall lineup and prices change from week to week, so the prices in this guide are for reference only.
For raw foods or foods that spoil if left out, check the hygiene before you buy.
In the rainy season the market may be cancelled because of showers or typhoons.
If you drive, roads nearby can be busy on Sunday mornings and parking is limited, so we recommend public transport or a ride-hailing taxi.
